prompt: In Go 1.27, what does `go get github.com/mattn/go-runewidth@v0.0.16` do?
hint: `go help get` says it in its first paragraph.

choices.text: Builds the package and installs the binary in `~/go/bin` for you
choices.why: That is what `go get` did before modules; installing is `go install` now.

choices.text: Requires that version in `go.mod` and downloads it
choices.why: Right. It adjusts the requirements and fetches the source, and builds nothing.

choices.text: Adds the import line to `main.go`
choices.why: The go command does not edit your source; `main.go` already imported the package.

choices.text: Copies the module's files into a `vendor` directory of your module
choices.why: That is `go mod vendor`, lesson 38; `go get` writes to the module cache, outside your module.

prompt: After `go get github.com/mattn/go-runewidth@latest`, the flag of Brazil went from 1 column to 2, with `main.go` untouched. Why?
hint: What did the upgrade replace?

choices.text: The `go` line in `go.mod` moved to a newer language version
choices.why: It stayed `go 1.27.1`; the language did not change, a dependency did.

choices.text: `go run` had kept an old binary in the cache
choices.why: The cache is rebuilt when a dependency changes; the first run was right for v0.0.16.

choices.text: A dependency changed: newer Unicode data
choices.why: Right. An upgrade replaces code your program runs, which is why you run it again afterwards.

choices.text: The terminal draws flags differently after a `go get`
choices.why: The output is ASCII escapes and a number the program computed; the terminal decided nothing.

prompt: `go list -m ___ all` prints each module with the newest published version beside it in square brackets.
hint: A one-letter flag.

prompt: Match each version query to the version `go get` picks.
hint: The table at the end of section 02.

pairs.right: The newest tagged release that is not retracted
The newest with the same major and minor as yours
No version: the requirement is removed

right_distractors: The newest commit on the default branch, tagged or not

prompt: `uniseg` is imported by 546 packages and `uax29/v2/graphemes` by 10. Why does section 03 still call the second the better bet?
hint: What does its source say about Unicode?

choices.text: `uniseg`'s licence forbids use in a program you sell
choices.why: Both printed `MIT License`, which allows that.

choices.text: Its tables follow Unicode 17.0.0, as this Go does, and `uniseg`'s stop at 15.0.0
choices.why: Right. For text the edition matters, and its last release, February 2026, is recent.

choices.text: `uniseg` pulls dozens of other modules into the build
choices.why: Its `go.mod` has no `require` line at all; neither candidate brings anything.

choices.text: Popular modules are the ones attackers target
choices.why: The section measured maintenance, not fame; popularity was called a measure of the past.

prompt: govulncheck said GO-2021-0113 is fixed in `golang.org/x/text` v0.3.7; `-show verbose` added GO-2022-1059, fixed in v0.3.8, and GO-2026-5970, fixed in v0.39.0. Which command ends all three?
hint: A fix version is a floor, not a target.

choices.text: `go get golang.org/x/text@v0.3.7`
choices.why: That ends the one your code calls and keeps the two it does not call yet.

choices.text: `go get golang.org/x/text@v0.3.8`
choices.why: Still below v0.39.0, so GO-2026-5970 stays.

choices.text: `go get golang.org/x/text@latest`
choices.why: Right. It went to v0.42.0, past every fix, and the scan then found nothing.

choices.text: `go get golang.org/x/text@none`
choices.why: The program imports `language` and would no longer build; removing is not upgrading.

prompt: Which of these are true of the govulncheck runs in section 03? Choose all that apply.
hint: Compare the first scan with the one after the upgrade.

choices.text: Exit status 3 meant that the code calls a vulnerable function
choices.why: Yes: the trace showed `main.go:12:28` calling `language.Parse`.

choices.text: It scanned the standard library of the Go that builds the module too
choices.why: Yes: `-show verbose` named `the go1.27.1 standard library`.

choices.text: `No vulnerabilities found` proves that the module has no flaws
choices.why: It says nothing in the database matches what the code calls, on that day.

choices.text: It read vuln.go.dev directly, as it does by default
choices.why: The lab cannot reach it; every scan named a local copy with `-db`.

prompt: How many requirements did one `go get github.com/gin-gonic/gin@v1.12.0` add to an empty module's `go.mod`?
hint: The command counted the `go: added` lines.

prompt: What makes `v0.1.0` of `example.com/ana/greet` exist?
hint: Look at what the author typed in `~/thirdparty-greet`.

choices.text: An upload to proxy.golang.org from an account
choices.why: There is no account and no upload; the proxy reads the repository when asked.

choices.text: A `version` line in the module's `go.mod`
choices.why: `go.mod` has no such line; the module's versions live outside the file.

choices.text: A git tag called `v0.1.0` in its repository
choices.why: Right. The proxy's `.info` for a real module even names the tag: `refs/tags/v0.0.16`.

choices.text: Its own page, created on pkg.go.dev
choices.why: pkg.go.dev shows documentation of what is published; it does not publish anything.

prompt: The first `go get` of `example.com/ana/greet` downloaded it and then failed with `404 Not Found` from sum.golang.org. Why?
hint: Read the `server response` line.

choices.text: The zip that the lab's own program wrote into the proxy was damaged
choices.why: The same zip was used a moment later, with `GONOSUMDB`, and it built.

choices.text: The database fetches the module itself, and nothing answers there
choices.why: Right: it tried `https://example.com/ana/greet?go-get=1` and got a 404.

choices.text: A `file://` proxy is allowed for listing versions, never for downloads
choices.why: `go help goproxy` says a `file://` URL can be a proxy, and the download line succeeded.

choices.text: `go.sum` had no line for the module yet
choices.why: That is the normal state before a first `go get`; the line is what the database was asked for.

prompt: Put the steps of releasing v1.1.0 in the lab in order, from the author's code to the importer's upgrade.
hint: Section 04, from `git tag` on.

prompt: A colleague's `go.sum` already lists `v0.1.0` when the author moves that tag to a new commit and the new contents are served. What does the colleague's next download of `v0.1.0` do?
hint: Section 04 did exactly this.

choices.text: Takes the new code without a word, since the tag name is the version
choices.why: The version name is the same, but go.sum holds the hash of the old contents.

choices.text: Warns that `v0.1.0` was retracted, then uses it
choices.why: Nothing was retracted; a retraction is a line the author publishes in a later version.

choices.text: Refuses it: `checksum mismatch`, then `SECURITY ERROR`
choices.why: Right. The go command cannot tell a careless author from an attacker, and refuses both.

choices.text: Offers `v0.1.1` instead, as the next patch
choices.why: No `v0.1.1` was ever tagged; the go command invents no versions.

prompt: What does `retract v1.1.0` in the `go.mod` of v1.1.1 do?
hint: Was v1.1.0 still downloadable afterwards?

choices.text: Deletes v1.1.0 from the proxy and from every module cache
choices.why: It deletes nothing: `go get ...@v1.1.0` still worked afterwards.

choices.text: Hides it from `@latest`, with a warning
choices.why: Right. It stays downloadable, marked `(retracted)`, with the author's reason in the warning.

choices.text: Moves the tag v1.1.0 to the fixed commit instead
choices.why: Moving a tag is what section 04 showed failing with `SECURITY ERROR`.

choices.text: Stops every module that requires v1.1.0 from building
choices.why: The importer on v1.1.0 still built and ran, and printed `Hello, AnaBia`.

prompt: From v2 on, the major version is part of the module ___, so `example.com/ana/greet` at v2 is imported as `example.com/ana/greet/v2`.
hint: The thing `go mod edit -module` changes.

prompt: `go list -m -u all` printed `example.com/ana/greet v1.1.1` with no brackets, although v2.0.0 exists. Why?
hint: Look at the two `@v/list` files.

choices.text: v2.0.0 was retracted when the author dropped the retraction
choices.why: `-dropretract` removed a line about v1.1.0; v2.0.0 was never retracted.

choices.text: `GONOSUMDB` hides versions that are not in the checksum database
choices.why: It skips verification and hides nothing; v1.1.1 is not in the database either.

choices.text: v2.0.0 belongs to another module path, and `-u` stays in one
choices.why: Right. Moving to v2 is a code change you make; no command makes it for you.

choices.text: The proxy listed v2.0.0 only once somebody asked for it
choices.why: The second `list` existed as soon as v2.0.0 was published, before any `go get`.

prompt: A module is at v1.4.0. Which of these changes call for v2.0.0 and a `/v2` path? Choose all that apply.
hint: Ask whether some caller's code stops compiling.

choices.text: An exported function now returns `(string, error)` instead of `string`
choices.why: Yes: `s := greet.Hello(name)` stops compiling, as section 05 said.

choices.text: A new exported function is added beside the old ones
choices.why: Nothing old changed; that is a minor release, v1.5.0.

choices.text: An exported function that callers use is removed
choices.why: Yes: every call to it stops compiling.

choices.text: A bug inside a function is fixed and its signature stays
choices.why: That is a patch, like v1.1.1's `" and "`.

prompt: A module at v0.9.0 wants to rename an exported function. What does its version number require?
hint: What does v0 promise?

choices.text: v1.0.0, since a breaking change needs a new major version
choices.why: That rule starts at v1; below it no release promises anything.

choices.text: A `/v1` suffix on the module path
choices.why: `go mod init` refused `/v1`: suffixes exist only for v2 or later.

choices.text: Just a new release, v0.10.0: v0 promises nothing
choices.why: Right. Importers of a v0 module accept that any release may break them.

choices.text: A `retract` of v0.9.0 in the next release
choices.why: v0.9.0 is not wrong, only replaced; a retraction is for a version nobody should use.

prompt: Your service's `go list -m -u all` shows `example.com/lib v1.4.0 (retracted) [v1.4.2]`. What is the right next step?
hint: The service still builds today.

choices.text: Nothing: a retracted version is refused at build time anyway
choices.why: The app built and ran on retracted v1.1.0; a retraction refuses nothing.

choices.text: Run `go mod tidy`, which removes retracted versions
choices.why: `tidy` matches `go.mod` to the imports; it does not change a version you need.

choices.text: Move to `example.com/lib/v2`, the only safe line
choices.why: Nothing says a v2 exists; the fix offered is v1.4.2, on the same path.

choices.text: Read the reason, then `go get` v1.4.2 and test
choices.why: Right. The reason is in the warning, and an upgrade is a change to check.

prompt: `go mod why -m github.com/clipperhouse/uax29/v2` printed a chain. Put it in the order it was printed, after the `#` line.
hint: From your code to the module.

prompt: Your company's modules live under `git.corp.example`, and their names must reach neither the public proxy nor the checksum database. Which setting does that?
hint: `go help private` describes one variable for both decisions.

choices.text: `GONOSUMDB=git.corp.example`
choices.why: That covers the checksum database only; downloads still go through the public proxy.

choices.text: `GOPRIVATE=git.corp.example`
choices.why: Right. It keeps those modules away from both the proxy and the checksum database.

choices.text: `GOSUMDB=off`
choices.why: That stops verifying every module, public ones too, and still uses the public proxy.

choices.text: `GOPROXY=off`
choices.why: That stops all downloads, so every public dependency breaks as well.
